items.stem: What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
options: A metaphor uses ‘like’; a simile does not
A simile compares using ‘like’ or ‘as’; a metaphor says one thing is another
A simile rhymes; a metaphor does not
items.answer: A simile compares using ‘like’ or ‘as’; a metaphor says one thing is another
items.markingKey: Simile: as still as stone. Metaphor: the river is a path of stone.

items.stem: In the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’ the writer uses the personification ‘nod’: ‘the fishing boats nod and creak and sway’ Explain what it suggests to the reader.
items.answer: the boats seem half-asleep, nodding like drowsy people, which continues the image of the harbour waking.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘nod’. Model point: the boats seem half-asleep, nodding like drowsy people, which continues the image of the harbour waking. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: ‘the kettle is always / about to sing’ (the poem ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’). What does the phrase ‘about to sing’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the kettle seems cheerful and alive, suggesting a warm, welcoming kitchen that is always ready for visitors.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘about to sing’. Model point: the kettle seems cheerful and alive, suggesting a warm, welcoming kitchen that is always ready for visitors. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Read ‘It drums on bus shelters,’ from the poem ‘City Rain’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Onomatopoeia (‘drums’): the word imitates the loud, rhythmic beat of rain on metal and plastic, bringing the noise of the city into the poem.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (onomatopoeia); 1 for selecting the key words ‘drums’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the word imitates the loud, rhythmic beat of rain on metal and plastic, bringing the noise of the city into the poem.

items.stem: Read ‘they lean on one another / like two old soldiers home from war’ from the poem ‘My Father’s Boots’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Simile (‘like two old soldiers home from war’): the boots seem tired, battered and supporting each other, suggesting hard work, endurance and perhaps loss.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (simile); 1 for selecting the key words ‘like two old soldiers home from war’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the boots seem tired, battered and supporting each other, suggesting hard work, endurance and perhaps loss.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from the poem ‘City Rain’: (i) ‘turns every gutter / into a gossiping river.’ (ii) ‘Umbrellas bloom like black flowers.’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Personification: the running water seems to chatter like people sharing news, capturing its constant, busy sound. (ii) Simile: umbrellas opening suddenly are compared to flowers opening, an unexpected, beautiful image in a grey city.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (personification; simile) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’. ‘The harbour wakes with a yawn of grey; / the fishing boats nod and creak and sway. / Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread / above the nets like cobwebs spread. / The water lies as still as stone / and holds each mast as if its own, / till a radio crackles, coughs and hums, / and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’ How does the poet present the harbour waking up? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Personification of harbour and boats as sleepy; quiet images (cobwebs, still as stone); sound builds from creaks to radio to engine roar; regular rhyming couplets give a gentle rhythm until the caesura and final short sentence.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Personification of harbour and boats as sleepy; quiet images (cobwebs, still as stone); sound builds from creaks to radio to engine roar; regular rhyming couplets give a gentle rhythm until the caesura and final short sentence.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘My Father’s Boots’. ‘By the back door my father’s boots / stand guard, still caked with field; / they lean on one another / like two old soldiers home from war. / He has not worn them since the spring. / Each morning I walk past them, slow, / and every morning they say nothing, / and every morning I say nothing back.’ How does the poet use the boots to explore the speaker’s feelings about their father? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Boots as a symbol of the absent father; personification (stand guard, say nothing); soldier simile; the short, blunt line about spring; repetition showing ongoing grief; restrained tone.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12 (reading). Indicative content: Boots as a symbol of the absent father; personification (stand guard, say nothing); soldier simile; the short, blunt line about spring; repetition showing ongoing grief; restrained tone.

items.stem: Which line contains personification?
options: The wind whispered secrets to the trees.
The wind was as cold as ice.
The wind blew from the north.
items.answer: The wind whispered secrets to the trees.
items.markingKey: The wind is given a human action (whispering).

items.stem: What is metre in poetry?
options: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line
The rhyme at the end of each line
items.answer: The regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line
items.markingKey: E.g. iambic metre: da-DUM da-DUM.

items.answer: the hissing sound of tyres on wet roads is captured exactly, and the short line mirrors the quick passing.

items.stem: Write a lullaby-style poem for a younger child about the night sky, using assonance and a regular rhythm. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model features: long soothing vowel sounds; regular metre; gentle rhyme; repetition or refrain. Example line: ‘The sizzle and spit of the pan on the flame.’
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a poem that uses sound devices skilfully and purposefully; sound and rhythm clearly support the subject and mood; well-shaped stanzas; middle band (3–4): some effective sound devices; some sense of rhythm; recognisable poetic form; lower band (1–2): few sound devices or used mechanically; little sense of form or rhythm. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: long soothing vowel sounds; regular metre; gentle rhyme; repetition or refrain.

items.stem: What is free verse?
options: Poetry without a regular rhyme scheme or metre
Poetry that is free to read online
Poetry that must rhyme in couplets
items.answer: Poetry without a regular rhyme scheme or metre
items.markingKey: Free verse follows natural speech rhythms; line breaks still matter.

items.stem: Explain how the use of caesura affects the way a reader reads these lines: ‘and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’
items.answer: Caesura: the full stop mid-line creates a pause that marks the sudden arrival of day.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying caesura; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the full stop mid-line creates a pause that marks the sudden arrival of day.

items.stem: These lines use rhyming couplet: ‘and when at last the thunder rolls, / we run outside with cups and bowls.’ Explain the effect of this structural choice.
items.answer: Rhyming couplet: the rhyme gives a satisfying, celebratory finish.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying rhyming couplet; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the rhyme gives a satisfying, celebratory finish.

items.stem: Identify the structural feature in these lines and analyse why the poet might have used it: ‘He has not worn them since the spring.’
items.answer: End-stopped line: the line ends with a full stop, so the sad fact stands alone and the reader pauses on it.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for end-stopped line; remaining marks for an analysis that links the structure to meaning or mood.

items.stem: Which connective is most useful for showing a similarity when comparing poems?
items.answer: Similarly
items.markingKey: Similarity: similarly, likewise, both. Difference: whereas, however, in contrast.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’: ‘In my grandmother’s kitchen / the kettle is always / about to sing. / Spices sleep in their jars, / cumin, turmeric, clove, / small brown secrets / she never wrote down. / Her hands are maps / of every meal she has made, / and when she laughs / the whole room / leans in to listen.’ and the poem ‘My Father’s Boots’: ‘By the back door my father’s boots / stand guard, still caked with field; / they lean on one another / like two old soldiers home from war. / He has not worn them since the spring. / Each morning I walk past them, slow, / and every morning they say nothing, / and every morning I say nothing back.’ Both poems are about family members and memory. Identify one similarity and one difference between them.
items.answer: Both use a household object or place to represent a family member (kitchen, boots) and both use personification. ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’ is warm and celebratory; ‘My Father’s Boots’ is restrained and sad, suggesting loss. Both use free verse, but the repetition in ‘My Father’s Boots’ creates a cycle of silence while the enjambment in ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’ creates warmth.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: valid similarity; valid difference; credit for supporting reference to both poems.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘City Rain’: ‘Rain arrives in the city / without knocking. / It drums on bus shelters, / slicks the streets to mirrors, / turns every gutter / into a gossiping river. / Umbrellas bloom like black flowers. / A taxi hisses past. / And for a moment / the whole loud city / holds its breath / and listens.’ and the poem ‘Drought’: ‘The sky is hard and white as bone, / the river is a path of stone; / the cattle stand with lowered heads / in fields of dry and dusty beds. / We watch the west for days on end / for any cloud the wind might send, / and when at last the thunder rolls, / we run outside with cups and bowls.’ Both poems are about weather and its effects on people. Identify one similarity and one difference between them.
items.answer: Both personify or vividly picture the weather. ‘City Rain’ shows rain as an everyday, noisy visitor in free verse; ‘Drought’ shows the desperate absence of rain in regular couplets, ending with joy when it finally arrives. Onomatopoeia dominates ‘City Rain’; harsh images (bone, stone) dominate ‘Drought’.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: valid similarity; valid difference; credit for supporting reference to both poems.

items.stem: Compare the use of sound in the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’ and the poem ‘City Rain’. Poem 1: ‘The harbour wakes with a yawn of grey; / the fishing boats nod and creak and sway. / Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread / above the nets like cobwebs spread. / The water lies as still as stone / and holds each mast as if its own, / till a radio crackles, coughs and hums, / and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’ Poem 2: ‘Rain arrives in the city / without knocking. / It drums on bus shelters, / slicks the streets to mirrors, / turns every gutter / into a gossiping river. / Umbrellas bloom like black flowers. / A taxi hisses past. / And for a moment / the whole loud city / holds its breath / and listens.’ Use a comparative connective and a short quotation from each poem.
items.answer: Both personify a place (the harbour wakes; the city holds its breath) and use onomatopoeia (crackles, drums, hisses). ‘Harbour at Dawn’ moves from silence to noise in rhyming couplets; ‘City Rain’ moves from noise to silence in free verse. Possible references: ‘wakes with a yawn’, ‘stitch the sky with silver thread’ / ‘without knocking’, ‘drums’.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: point about poem 1 with evidence; comparative point about poem 2 with evidence; explanation of the effect of each; comparative connective used.

items.stem: Both poems explore change and the passing of time. Compare how the poets use language in these lines. Poem 1 (the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’): ‘the fishing boats nod and creak and sway’ Poem 2 (the poem ‘The Tree Outside My Window’): ‘a green rumour spreads / from twig to twig.’ Write a comparative paragraph using point, evidence and explanation for each.
items.answer: Poem 1 uses personification (‘nod’): the boats seem half-asleep, nodding like drowsy people, which continues the image of the harbour waking. Poem 2 uses metaphor (‘a green rumour’): new buds appear gradually like gossip passing from person to person, a fresh image of spring spreading. A comparative link (e.g. ‘whereas’, ‘similarly’) should connect the two to the theme of change and the passing of time.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: technique and effect for poem 1; technique and effect for poem 2; comparative connective and a judgement linking both to the theme.

items.stem: Poem 1, the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’: ‘The harbour wakes with a yawn of grey; / the fishing boats nod and creak and sway. / Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread / above the nets like cobwebs spread. / The water lies as still as stone / and holds each mast as if its own, / till a radio crackles, coughs and hums, / and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’ Poem 2, the poem ‘The Tree Outside My Window’: ‘In January it is a skeleton, / all elbows and knuckles, / scratching at the glass. / By April it has changed its mind: / a green rumour spreads / from twig to twig. / July, and it is a crowded room / of leaves and gossip, / of birds that never sleep. / And I, who have not moved all year, / watch it become / three different trees.’ Compare the ways in which the two poets explore change and the passing of time. Write about language, structure and the effect on the reader.
items.answer: ‘Harbour at Dawn’ shows change over one morning using personification and building sound; ‘The Tree Outside My Window’ shows change over a year through seasonal stanzas and metaphor. The harbour poem ends with the arrival of day; the tree poem ends by turning to the speaker.

Indicative content: ‘Harbour at Dawn’ shows change over one morning using personification and building sound; ‘The Tree Outside My Window’ shows change over a year through seasonal stanzas and metaphor. items.stem: What is imagery?

Language that creates pictures or sensations in the reader’s mind
The number of stanzas in a poem
items.answer: Language that creates pictures or sensations in the reader’s mind
items.markingKey: Imagery appeals to the senses and includes similes, metaphors and personification.

items.answer: wet streets become shiny reflective surfaces, suggesting light and colour reflected everywhere; ‘slicks’ suggests speed and smoothness.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘Drought’. ‘The sky is hard and white as bone, / the river is a path of stone; / the cattle stand with lowered heads / in fields of dry and dusty beds. / We watch the west for days on end / for any cloud the wind might send, / and when at last the thunder rolls, / we run outside with cups and bowls.’ How does the poet show the effects of drought and the relief when it ends?
items.answer: Similes and metaphors of bone and stone; sad image of cattle; alliteration of dry/dusty; regular rhyme and steady metre suggest the long wait; final couplet shifts to joy and action.

items.stem: Read the poem ‘The Tree Outside My Window’. ‘In January it is a skeleton, / all elbows and knuckles, / scratching at the glass. / By April it has changed its mind: / a green rumour spreads / from twig to twig. / July, and it is a crowded room / of leaves and gossip, / of birds that never sleep. / And I, who have not moved all year, / watch it become / three different trees.’ How does the poet use the structure and imagery of the poem to show change?
items.answer: Three seasonal stanzas (January, April, July) give a chronological structure; metaphors move from death (skeleton) to rumour to crowded room; final stanza turns to the motionless speaker – a shift that invites reflection.
items.markingKey: Level-marked: top band (4–5) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2–3) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [5]

items.stem: Read the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’: ‘The harbour wakes with a yawn of grey; / the fishing boats nod and creak and sway. / Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread / above the nets like cobwebs spread. / The water lies as still as stone / and holds each mast as if its own, / till a radio crackles, coughs and hums, / and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’ and the poem ‘City Rain’: ‘Rain arrives in the city / without knocking. / It drums on bus shelters, / slicks the streets to mirrors, / turns every gutter / into a gossiping river. / Umbrellas bloom like black flowers. / A taxi hisses past. / And for a moment / the whole loud city / holds its breath / and listens.’ Both poems are about places coming to life. Identify one similarity and one difference between them.
items.answer: Both personify a place (the harbour wakes; the city holds its breath) and use onomatopoeia (crackles, drums, hisses). ‘Harbour at Dawn’ moves from silence to noise in rhyming couplets; ‘City Rain’ moves from noise to silence in free verse.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: valid similarity; valid difference; credit for supporting reference to both poems.

items.stem: Line from the poem ‘City Rain’: ‘the whole loud city / holds its breath / and listens.’ Line from the poem ‘Drought’: ‘in fields of dry and dusty beds.’ Explain one similarity or difference in the way these two lines create an effect.
items.answer: The first uses personification, whereas the second uses alliteration: the city becomes a person pausing in wonder, creating a calm, reflective ending after the noise. By contrast/similarly, the hard ‘d’ sounds stress the dryness and make the line sound heavy and tired.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for identifying the technique in each line; 1 for a comparative point about effect; credit any valid comparison.

items.stem: Both poems explore places coming to life. Compare how the poets use language in these lines. Poem 1 (the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’): ‘Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread’ Poem 2 (the poem ‘City Rain’): ‘It drums on bus shelters,’ Write a comparative paragraph using point, evidence and explanation for each.
items.answer: Poem 1 uses metaphor (‘stitch the sky with silver thread’): the gulls’ flight paths become threads sewn across the sky, suggesting delicate, criss-crossing movement and light catching their wings. Poem 2 uses onomatopoeia (‘drums’): the word imitates the loud, rhythmic beat of rain on metal and plastic, bringing the noise of the city into the poem. A comparative link (e.g. ‘whereas’, ‘similarly’) should connect the two to the theme of places coming to life.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: technique and effect for poem 1; technique and effect for poem 2; comparative connective and a judgement linking both to the theme.

items.stem: Poem 1, the poem ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’: ‘In my grandmother’s kitchen / the kettle is always / about to sing. / Spices sleep in their jars, / cumin, turmeric, clove, / small brown secrets / she never wrote down. / Her hands are maps / of every meal she has made, / and when she laughs / the whole room / leans in to listen.’ Poem 2, the poem ‘My Father’s Boots’: ‘By the back door my father’s boots / stand guard, still caked with field; / they lean on one another / like two old soldiers home from war. / He has not worn them since the spring. / Each morning I walk past them, slow, / and every morning they say nothing, / and every morning I say nothing back.’ Compare the ways in which the two poets explore family members and memory. Write about language, structure and the effect on the reader.
items.answer: Both use a household object or place to represent a family member (kitchen, boots) and both use personification. ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’ is warm and celebratory; ‘My Father’s Boots’ is restrained and sad, suggesting loss. Both use free verse, but the repetition in ‘My Father’s Boots’ creates a cycle of silence while the enjambment in ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’ creates warmth.

Both use free verse, but the repetition in ‘My Father’s Boots’ creates a cycle of silence while the enjambment in ‘Grandmother’s Kitchen’ creates warmth. items.stem: Compare the structure and form of the poems in the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’ and the poem ‘The Tree Outside My Window’. Poem 1: ‘The harbour wakes with a yawn of grey; / the fishing boats nod and creak and sway. / Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread / above the nets like cobwebs spread. / The water lies as still as stone / and holds each mast as if its own, / till a radio crackles, coughs and hums, / and the first bright engine roars. Day comes.’ Poem 2: ‘In January it is a skeleton, / all elbows and knuckles, / scratching at the glass. / By April it has changed its mind: / a green rumour spreads / from twig to twig. / July, and it is a crowded room / of leaves and gossip, / of birds that never sleep. / And I, who have not moved all year, / watch it become / three different trees.’ Use a comparative connective and a short quotation from each poem.
items.answer: ‘Harbour at Dawn’ shows change over one morning using personification and building sound; ‘The Tree Outside My Window’ shows change over a year through seasonal stanzas and metaphor. The harbour poem ends with the arrival of day; the tree poem ends by turning to the speaker. Possible references: ‘wakes with a yawn’, ‘stitch the sky with silver thread’ / ‘a skeleton’, ‘scratching at the glass’.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: point about poem 1 with evidence; comparative point about poem 2 with evidence; explanation of the effect of each; comparative connective used.
